questions.q: What are the three general types of production?
options: Mass production, mass customization and customization
questions.explain: Each type balances cost and how individual the product is.
questions.evidence: In general, there are three types of production: mass production, mass customization, and customization.

questions.q: What is mass production?
options: Making each product to one customer's wishes
Producing goods only after a customer orders them
Manufacturing many identical goods at once
questions.explain: It was a product of the Industrial Revolution.
questions.evidence: One for All: Mass Production Mass production, manufacturing many identical goods at once, was a product of the Industrial Revolution.

questions.q: What does mass production emphasise?
options: Low manufacturing costs through uniform products and repetitive, standardised processes
questions.explain: Uniform, standardised processes keep costs low.
questions.evidence: The emphasis in mass production is on keeping manufacturing costs low by producing uniform products using repetitive and standardized processes.

questions.q: How does customization differ from mass customization?
options: In customization each product or service produced is unique
questions.explain: Customization is the opposite of mass production.
questions.evidence: Unlike mass customization, each product or service produced is unique.

questions.q: What does quality control involve?
options: Creating quality standards, producing goods that meet them and measuring results against them
Inspecting goods only at the end of the line
questions.explain: It needs company-wide dedication, not just end-of-line inspection.
questions.evidence: Quality control involves creating quality standards, producing goods that meet them, and measuring finished goods and services against them.

questions.q: Who was the first to say that quality control should be a company-wide goal?
questions.explain: Deming believed quality starts with top management.
questions.evidence: Edwards Deming, an American management consultant, was the first to say that quality control should be a company-wide goal.

questions.q: What does Total Quality Management (TQM) emphasise?
options: Using quality principles in all aspects of production and operations
questions.explain: TQM is Deming's concept.
questions.evidence: Deming’s concept of Total Quality Management (TQM) emphasizes the use of quality principles in all aspects of a company’s production and operations.

questions.q: Why do defective products raise costs?
options: They are always sold at a higher price
They reduce the need for inspections
questions.explain: Quality problems waste resources.
questions.evidence: Defective products waste materials and time, increasing costs.

questions.q: What is kaizen often considered in lean production?
options: The "building block" of all lean production methods
questions.explain: Kaizen means rapid improvement processes and continual improvement.
questions.evidence: Kaizen , or rapid improvement processes, often is considered to be the "building block" of all lean production methods.

questions.q: What does kaizen focus on?
options: Eliminating waste, improving productivity and sustaining continual improvement
questions.explain: Lean production is founded on continual improvement.
questions.evidence: Kaizen focuses on eliminating waste, improving productivity, and achieving sustained continual improvement in targeted activities and processes of an organization.

questions.q: How quickly does a kaizen team often implement chosen improvements?
options: Only at the end of the financial year
Often within 72 hours of starting the kaizen event
questions.explain: Kaizen events favour rapid, low-capital solutions.
questions.evidence: The team works to implement chosen improvements rapidly (often within 72 hours of initiating the kaizen event), typically focusing on solutions that do not involve large capital outlays.

questions.q: Which techniques does a kaizen team use to find waste quickly?
questions.explain: These analytical techniques identify waste in a targeted process.
questions.evidence: The team uses analytical techniques, such as value stream mapping and "the 5 whys", to identify opportunities quickly to eliminate waste in a targeted process or production area.

questions.q: What are the five pillars of 5S?
options: Sort, set in order, shine, standardize and sustain
Save, sell, ship, store and scan
Speed, safety, size, stock and service
Plan, do, check, act and repeat
questions.explain: 5S organises, cleans and sustains a productive workplace.
questions.evidence: The 5S pillars, Sort ( Seiri ), Set in Order ( Seiton ), Shine ( Seiso ), Standardize ( Seiketsu ), and Sustain ( Shitsuke ), provide a methodology for organizing, cleaning, developing, and sustaining a productive work environment.

questions.q: What does the first S, Sort, focus on?
options: Eliminating items that are not needed for current production
questions.explain: Sorting reclaims space and removes broken tools and scrap.
questions.evidence: Sort, the first S, focuses on eliminating unnecessary items from the workplace that are not needed for current production operations.

questions.q: What is "red tagging" in 5S?
options: A visual method to evaluate whether each item in a work area is needed
questions.explain: Red tags identify unneeded items so they can be dealt with.
questions.evidence: An effective visual method to identify these unneeded items is called "red tagging", which involves evaluating the necessity of each item in a work area and dealing with it appropriately.

questions.q: What does just-in-time (JIT) enable a company to do?
options: Produce what customers want, when they want it, in the amount they want
questions.explain: JIT reduces inventory and work-in-process.
questions.evidence: JIT enables a company to produce the products its customers want, when they want them, in the amount they want.

questions.q: What is kanban used for in JIT?
options: Physical cues that signal the need to move materials or produce components
questions.explain: Kanban (sometimes reusable containers) ensure only what is needed gets produced.
questions.evidence: JIT frequently relies on the use of physical inventory control cues (or kanban) to signal the need to move raw materials or produce new components from the previous process.

questions.q: How do JIT techniques make flow between processes smoother?
options: By producing everything in one big batch
By stopping production whenever stock is low
By levelling production, spreading it evenly over time
questions.explain: Levelled production fosters smooth flow.
questions.evidence: JIT techniques work to level production, spreading production evenly over time to foster a smooth flow between processes.

questions.q: What does Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) seek to do?
options: Leave all maintenance to an outside contractor
Engage all levels and functions to maximise the effectiveness of production equipment
Reduce the number of maintenance checks
questions.explain: TPM involves everyone, not just the maintenance department.
questions.evidence: Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) seeks to engage all levels and functions in an organization to maximize the overall effectiveness of production equipment.

questions.q: What is autonomous maintenance in TPM?
options: Training workers to take care of the equipment and machines they work with
questions.explain: It is a key aspect of TPM.
questions.evidence: Autonomous maintenance, a key aspect of TPM, trains and focuses workers to take care of the equipment and machines with which they work.

questions.q: What are the ultimate goals of TPM?
options: Zero equipment breakdowns and zero product defects
questions.explain: These goals improve use of assets and plant capacity.
questions.evidence: The ultimate goals of TPM are zero equipment breakdowns and zero product defects, which lead to improved utilization of production assets and plant capacity.

questions.q: Who developed Six Sigma?
questions.explain: It drew on statistical quality control and data analysis.
questions.evidence: Six Sigma was developed by Motorola in the 1990s, drawing on well-established statistical quality control techniques and data analysis methods.

questions.q: What does a Six Sigma quality level equate to?
questions.explain: It represents high quality and minimal variability.
questions.evidence: A Six Sigma quality level equates to approximately 3.4 defects per million opportunities, representing high quality and minimal process variability.

questions.q: What does a sigma quality level indicate?
options: How many employees a plant has
How often defects are likely to occur
questions.explain: Higher sigma levels mean fewer defects.
questions.evidence: A sigma quality level serves as an indicator of how often defects are likely to occur in processes, parts, or products.

questions.q: Who first applied statistical methods to quality control?
options: Walter A. Shewhart of Bell Telephone Laboratories
questions.explain: His 1924 memorandum sketched a modern control chart.
questions.evidence: He issued a memorandum on May 16, 1924 that featured a sketch of a modern control chart.

questions.q: What is process control?
options: Actively changing the process based on the results of process monitoring
questions.explain: Interventions can be based on engineering judgement or be automated.
questions.evidence: Process Control is the active changing of the process based on the results of process monitoring.

questions.q: What does a process engineer do when a process is out of control?
options: Ignores it until the next audit
Looks for an assignable cause by following the out-of-control action plan (OCAP)
questions.explain: The OCAP is linked to the control chart.
questions.evidence: If the process is out-of-control, the process engineer looks for an assignable cause by following the out-of-control action plan (OCAP) associated with the control chart.

questions.q: What does the centre line of a control chart represent?
options: The mean value for the in-control process
questions.explain: Upper and lower control limits are drawn around it.
questions.evidence: In general, the chart contains a center line that represents the mean value for the in-control process.

questions.q: What are the two horizontal lines drawn on a control chart besides the centre line?
options: The upper control limit (UCL) and the lower control limit (LCL)
The price line and the cost line
The start date and end date
The supplier line and the customer line
questions.explain: Points outside these limits suggest an assignable cause.
questions.evidence: Two other horizontal lines, called the upper control limit ( UCL ) and the lower control limit ( LCL ), are also shown on the chart.

questions.q: What should you do if a point falls outside the control limits?
options: Delete the point from the data
Search for an assignable cause of the variation
questions.explain: Points outside the limits signal possible special causes.
questions.evidence: We would be searching for an assignable cause if a point would fall outside these limits.

questions.q: For a normal distribution, how likely is a point outside ±3σ?
questions.explain: That is why 3-sigma limits rarely give false alarms.
questions.evidence: We know that, for a normal distribution, the probability of encountering a point outside ± 3 σ is 0.3%.

questions.q: What are attributes in quality control?
options: Measurements such as thickness in millimetres
Quality characteristics from classifying or counting, such as defective or non-defective
questions.explain: Attributes data arise when classifying or counting observations.
questions.evidence: Quality characteristics of that type are called attributes.

questions.q: What does process capability compare?
options: The output of an in-control process with the specification limits
questions.explain: Capability indices form the comparison.
questions.evidence: Process capability compares the output of an in-control process to the specification limits by using capability indices .

questions.q: What is a capable process?
options: One that never needs a control chart
One that has the lowest cost
One where almost all measurements fall inside the specification limits
questions.explain: Capability compares natural variability with the specification limits.
questions.evidence: A process where almost all the measurements fall inside the specification limits is a capable process.

questions.q: In the lesson's table, if the specification width (USL − LSL) equals 8σ, what is Cp?
questions.explain: Cp 1.00, 1.33, 1.66 and 2.00 correspond to 6, 8, 10 and 12 σ.
